steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Evaluation means making judgements about a text and supporting your opinions with evidence. You assess how successfully the writer achieves their purpose.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.body: Decide your overall opinion - agree, disagree, or partially agree Step 2: Find evidence that supports your view Step 3: Analyse how the writer achieves the effect Step 4: Consider alternative viewpoints if appropriate Step 5: Reach a conclusion

steps.title: Examiner's Tip
steps.body: This is worth 20 marks - the most on the paper. Spend about 20-25 minutes on it. Make sure you give a clear opinion and back it up with detailed analysis of the text.

steps.title: Evaluation Exam Strategy
steps.body: This is AQA Paper 1 Q4 - the highest-mark question at 20 marks. Spend 20-25 minutes on it. Start by deciding your position: agree, disagree, or partially agree. Then build your argument with 3-4 PEEL paragraphs, each one analysing a different method the writer uses. Include a counter-argument or concession to show balanced thinking. End with a clear conclusion. Examiners reward confident, well-supported judgements - don't sit on the fence, but do show you've considered the text fully.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: What does "evaluate" mean in the context of English Language? | How should you structure an evaluation response? | Why is it important to use evidence in evaluation?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: To make a judgement about how effective or successful a text is, supported by evidence and analysis. | Start with your opinion, use PEEL paragraphs with evidence and analysis, consider alternative views, and reach a conclusion. | Evidence proves your opinion is based on the text rather than just personal preference - it shows you can support your ideas.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Start by deciding your overall opinion Make your judgement clear from the start Use "I agree/disagree" language confidently Support every point with specific evidence Analyse language AND structure where relevant Consider both sides for a balanced argument This is a high-mark question - manage your time well
